title: Silicon Shield, Tennessee Fallout
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

President Donald Trump’s effort to strengthen America’s semiconductor supply chain may instead threaten one of its few domestic polysilicon plants. Wacker Chemie, a German manufacturer, is considering closing its Charleston, Tennessee, facility after the administration’s latest trade measures reportedly drove away its final two customers. The plant employs about 600 people and produces high-purity polysilicon used in semiconductor chips and solar panels.

The White House measures, announced in August and scheduled to take effect in December, impose tariffs and price floors on imported polysilicon ingots, wafers, cells, and solar panels. Their stated goal is to encourage American production and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, particularly China. However, the rules do not distinguish between products made with American polysilicon and those using cheaper material from abroad. Consequently, downstream manufacturers have little reason to buy the American product, which can cost four times as much.

Wacker says the proclamation, in its current form, does not effectively support the use of United States-made polysilicon. The company is discussing possible solutions with administration officials, but it expects to decide the Tennessee plant’s future within weeks. Its shares fell following the report.

The case illustrates the risks of poorly targeted industrial policy. Tariffs can protect domestic companies only when regulations account for the entire supply chain and create genuine demand for American inputs. Otherwise, they may raise costs without changing purchasing decisions.

Supporters of stronger trade barriers are urging Washington to reward companies that buy domestically produced polysilicon. They warn that failure to do so could deepen Chinese dominance in both solar and semiconductor materials, creating economic and national-security vulnerabilities. The administration can still offer company-specific incentives, but unless it revises implementation, a policy designed to reshore strategic manufacturing could accelerate the loss of a major American facility and hundreds of skilled jobs in Tennessee.

Source: Reuters
